title: Correlation and causation
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:39Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The closest bank point, mat-correlation-causation, covers correlation versus causation and third factors, but it says a reasonable explanation and ruled-out third factors can support causation, not that only a controlled experiment can, which is the central claim of the new point.

draft.title: Correlation and causation
card: Two variables can be correlated, which means they move together, without one causing the other.
Another variable may explain both. This is a lurking variable. Hot weather raises both ice cream sales and drowning numbers, so the two are correlated.
Observing data alone cannot show cause. It shows only that variables are associated.
A controlled experiment can show cause. Subjects are assigned to groups at random and only the explanatory variable is changed, so other factors are spread evenly across the groups.
draft.remember: Correlation is not causation. Only a controlled experiment can show cause.

a.q: A survey finds that towns with more pools have more sunburn cases. Which is the best conclusion?
opts: The two are associated, but cause is not shown
Pools cause sunburn in these towns
Sunburn causes towns to build more pools
Pools and sunburn have no association
a.why: The survey observed the towns and did not run an experiment, so it cannot show cause. A lurking variable such as hot weather may explain both. Pools causing sunburn is only one possible explanation.
a.clue: Was anything controlled in this survey?

b.q: Leila wants to test if a new study app raises marks. Which plan could show that the app causes higher marks?
opts: Randomly give the app to half of a class and compare
Compare marks of students who chose to use the app
Ask students if they think the app helps their marks
Check if app use and marks are highly correlated
b.why: Random assignment spreads other factors evenly across both groups, so a difference in marks can be put down to the app. Students who choose the app may already be more motivated, so comparing them cannot show cause.
b.clue: Who decides which students get the app?

a.best: The two are associated, but cause is not shown

b.best: Randomly give the app to half of a class and compare
